case_study_insert.main_stem: Seabrook Coastal Hotels (SCH) is a private limited company in the hospitality and hotel sector, employing a workforce of 160. Founded in 2004 by Dana Whitmore, the group operates three coastal hotels along the shoreline and uses a flat organisational structure with autocratic leadership from Dana Whitmore. SCH plans to invest $1,200,000 in refurbishing its flagship cliff-top hotel and adding a new wedding and events wing, financed by a $750,000 twelve-year bank loan and $450,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $2,490,000 a year, a variable cost of $62 a unit and a selling price of $145, and currently produces 58,000 units a year (one unit is one occupied room-night). SCH faces two problems: seasonal staff turnover has reached 34% and absenteeism stands at 10%, and wedding enquiries are being lost to a rival events venue.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations Log — Q3 2026: SCH's hotels sold 15,080 room-nights at an average occupancy of 71%, up from 63% a year ago. Wedding and events bookings reached 46 this quarter, up from 29 a year ago. Guest complaints fell from 34 to 19 per month, and average check-in time is 6 minutes. Market research of 800 guests found 58% would pay up to $25 more per night for a refurbished sea-view room, and review scores average 8.4 out of 10 across 2,300 reviews. Training needs analysis shows 28 of 160 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new wedding catering systems; college courses cost $1,100 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Seabrook Coastal Hotels as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 5.0% to 5.75%, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans such as SCH's planned expansion. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.9% from $12.15 to $12.85 per hour from April 2026, raising the total wage bill for seasonal and permanent hotel staff. (3) Wholesale food and energy input costs have risen 9.8% year-on-year, while consumer spending on domestic coastal holidays grew 4.2% in the same period.

questions.question_text: SCH plans to finance part of its refurbishment and wedding wing with a twelve-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for SCH of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Using retained profit avoids all interest charges on the $750,000 bank loan, so the twelve-year commitment does not add to SCH's $2,490,000 fixed costs at a time when food and energy costs have already risen 9.8%. Every dollar SCH saves on interest can be redirected to the refurbishment and to absorbing the 5.9% rise in the minimum wage to $12.85, protecting the group's $83 contribution ($145 − $62) on each occupied room-night and keeping room rates at $145 competitive for domestic coastal tourists, whose spending grew 4.2% this year.

Point 2: Retained profit involves no collateral, so Dana Whitmore does not risk losing the flagship cliff-top hotel or its new wedding and events wing if trading becomes difficult during quieter winter months. It also preserves complete ownership and control for SCH's existing shareholders, avoids the lender imposing conditions on how the wing is run, and leaves the option of a bank loan open later if wedding bookings exceed the 46 already recorded in Q3 2026.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Seabrook Coastal Hotels and its expansion decision.

questions.question_text: SCH is launching its refurbished sea-view rooms and new wedding and events wing. Consider a national television campaign, local newspaper advertising, or social media influencer marketing aimed at wedding planners and couples. Which should SCH choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Television campaign: A national TV campaign would give SCH the widest possible reach and would build fast, prestigious awareness of the refurbished cliff-top hotel across the country. However, production and airtime costs are extremely high for a 160-employee family-influenced private limited company already financing $750,000 of the $1,200,000 refurbishment with a bank loan, and much of a national audience would never book a coastal wedding at SCH; spend would be wasted outside its catchment.

Local newspaper advertising: Local newspapers are cheap, reach the regional audience most likely to book sea-view weekend breaks and local weddings, and suit a grand-opening offer for the wing. Their limitation is narrow circulation and an ageing readership, so they would do little for the 58% of researched guests willing to pay more for sea-view rooms who live further afield, and they cannot showcase the wing visually in a competitive events market.

Social media influencer marketing: Partnering with wedding-planner influencers and coastal-lifestyle creators targets exactly the couples researching venues online, reaches a national audience for far less than TV, and provides measurable engagement, booking enquiries and review traction; the 8.4 average review score and rising occupancy of 71% give influencers strong proof to share. It depends on influencer authenticity and takes longer to compound than TV, but the cost per engaged couple is low.

Recommendation: SCH should choose social media influencer marketing. It speaks directly to wedding planners and couples nationally at a cost SCH can afford alongside its bank loan, reinforces the review-driven reputation (8.4/10), and shows the wing visually. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a $1,200,000 project financed partly by debt; local newspapers are rejected as too narrow for a tiered national events market, though SCH can add low-cost local print for community weddings once the launch quietens.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of SCH with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of SCH with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and newspaper advertising are rejected.

questions.question_text: SCH's seasonal staff turnover has reached 34% and absenteeism stands at 10%. Explain two benefits for SCH of introducing off-the-job training for its seasonal hotel staff.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Off-the-job training, such as the college courses costing $1,100 per employee, gives seasonal staff recognised qualifications and structured skills before the summer peak, which raises their confidence, morale and sense of being valued beyond a casual contract. This directly attacks SCH's 34% seasonal staff turnover, because staff who feel invested in are far more likely to return each season, saving SCH repeated recruitment and induction costs while its flat structure depends on experienced supervisors being available.

Point 2: Training away from the hotel — for example in wedding catering systems and customer service — means the 28 staff who have not completed on-the-job training can learn without disrupting guests in the refurbished rooms. Skilled, certified staff make fewer errors, supporting the fall in complaints from 34 to 19 per month, protecting the 71% occupancy that finances the $1,200,000 refurbishment, and ensuring the wedding and events wing opens with capable, motivated teams rather than rushed-on casual labour.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to SCH's seasonal turnover, absenteeism and expansion.

questions.question_text: SCH is opening its wedding and events wing and needs staff for it. Consider recruiting more seasonal temporary staff or training and promoting existing permanent staff to lead the wing. Which should SCH choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Seasonal temporary staff: Hiring seasonal workers matches SCH's existing summer-peak pattern and keeps immediate wage costs low, which suits a wing that will be busiest at weekends and during wedding season. It gives SCH flexibility to scale up for large weddings, and wages rise only with the 5.9% minimum wage increase rather than with full-year salaries. However, seasonal staff already churn at 34%, the 10% absenteeism is worst among casuals, and weddings demand consistently high service and reliability; re-training each season would overload supervisors already managing the refurbishment.

Promote and train existing permanent staff: Promoting from within rewards loyalty, fills the 28-person training gap identified in the needs analysis, and retains SCH's service culture and 8.4 review score for critical events. Promotion satisfies esteem needs (Maslow) and reduces labour turnover by giving staff a career path into events management. The costs are higher short-term wages, the need to backfill roles and the risk that promoted staff need new skills they do not yet have.

Decision: SCH should choose training and promoting existing permanent staff to lead the wedding and events wing, supported by seasonal casuals only at peak weekends. Weddings are high-stakes events where Dana Whitmore's autocratic flat structure needs trusted, committed leaders who know the hotel; reliance on seasonal staff is rejected because it has already produced 34% turnover and 10% absenteeism and would damage the reviews that win premium sea-view bookings. Seasonal hires alone are too unreliable; full-time promotion alone is also rejected as too rigid for weekend peaks, so a permanent core with casual weekend support is best.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two staffing approaches with limited application to SCH.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both staffing options in the context of SCH.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options in the context of SCH with a well-justified decision covering reliability, motivation, cost and wedding-service risk.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how SCH's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $2,490,000 ÷ ($145 − $62) = $2,490,000 ÷ $83 = 30,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 30,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $145 − $62 = $83. Answer: contribution per unit is $83.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways SCH's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. SCH can compare the 30,000-unit break-even output with actual production of 58,000 units to confirm a margin of safety of 28,000 room-nights, showing the hotels trade far above break-even and can support the $1,200,000 refurbishment repayments on the $750,000 bank loan safely through quieter winter months.
2. With $83 contribution per unit, management can test the effect of a weekday discount for domestic coastal-holiday travellers, for example a $15 cut to $130 would reduce contribution to $68 ($130 − $62), letting SCH judge whether extra occupancy needed to offset it is realistic given consumer spending on coastal holidays grew 4.2%.
3. Knowing fixed costs of $2,490,000 and $83 contribution helps SCH set wedding and events wing room-rate and package targets, ensuring the wing contributes enough to cover its share of loan interest after the interest rate rose to 5.75%, before committing to further marketing spend.
4. Managers can use unit cost data ($2,490,000 ÷ 58,000 units + $62 = $104.93 a unit) to benchmark each of the three hotels, identify which property drives the food-waste and energy overspend highlighted by the 9.8% input-cost rise, and decide whether to renegotiate supplier contracts or raise sea-view rates, which 58% of guests said they would accept at up to $25 more.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 30,000 units a year, computed as $2,490,000 fixed costs divided by $83 contribution per room-night (selling price $145 less variable cost $62). At the current 58,000-unit output, SCH operates a margin of safety of 28,000 units, so room-night revenue comfortably covers both fixed and variable costs. (ii) Contribution per unit = $83 per occupied room-night, which is what every sold room-night contributes toward fixed costs and, after that, profit. (iii) Four applied uses: first, tracking the margin of safety ahead of the $750,000 bank loan repayments for the flagship refurbishment; second, modelling weekday coastal-holiday discounts where each $15 price cut reduces contribution to $68 ($130 − $62); third, setting rate and package targets for the new wedding and events wing so packages cover fixed costs after interest at 5.75%; fourth, unit-cost benchmarking at $104.93 ($2,490,000 ÷ 58,000 + $62) to locate food and energy overspends behind the 9.8% input-cost rise. Together these uses let Dana Whitmore test whether the hotel and wing stay above break-even through the quieter winter months while the $1,200,000 refurbishment is delivered.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate SCH's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has SCH's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.53 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.83 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.97 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.36 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $210,000 inventories + $240,000 trade receivables + $130,000 cash = $580,000; 2025 current assets = $165,000 + $285,000 + $190,000 = $640,000. Current liabilities were $380,000 in 2024 and fell to $350,000 in 2025. 2024: $580,000 ÷ $380,000 = 1.53; 2025: $640,000 ÷ $350,000 = 1.83. The stricter measure excluding inventories: 2024 = ($580,000 − $210,000) ÷ $380,000 = $370,000 ÷ $380,000 = 0.97; 2025 = ($640,000 − $165,000) ÷ $350,000 = $475,000 ÷ $350,000 = 1.36.

Evaluation: Liquidity has strengthened considerably. Current assets cover short-term debts much more comfortably, aided by inventories falling from $210,000 to $165,000 and cash rising to $190,000, showing tighter stock control in hotel kitchens and stronger room-revenue collection. The stricter measure improved from below 1.0 to 1.36, meaning SCH can now meet short-term debts without selling food and beverage stock — important while it services a $750,000 twelve-year bank loan at a base rate of 5.75%. Two cautions remain: trade receivables rose from $240,000 to $285,000, so corporate wedding and events deposits must be collected promptly, and current liabilities of $350,000 still exceed cash alone.

Conclusion: SCH's financial position has improved. Both measures show stronger short-term solvency in 2025 and the improvement is not reliant on inventory. SCH should maintain the gain by tightening credit control on events deposits and preserving cash to fund the $1,200,000 refurbishment, which protects the occupancy and wedding bookings underpinning it.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether SCH's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for SCH of refurbishing with sustainable eco-friendly materials for its flagship cliff-top hotel.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Sustainable refurbishment matches the 58% of researched guests willing to pay up to $25 more per night for a refurbished sea-view room, many of whom actively choose hotels with credible environmental credentials. SCH can therefore hold or raise its $145 room rate, protecting the $83 contribution ($145 − $62) per occupied room-night even as food and energy costs rose 9.8%, and the eco-story strengthens the 8.4 review score and SCH's bid to win premium coastal wedding contracts over rival venues.

Disadvantage: Eco-materials such as certified timber, low-energy glazing and water-saving systems typically cost more than conventional fittings, so part of the $1,200,000 budget — already stretched by the $750,000 bank loan — would be consumed before the wing opens. If sustainable fittings fail early or deliver poorer soundproofing or durability, SCH's complaints (already down, but still 19 per month) could rise again, damaging the guest experience precisely when it is trying to convert the 71% occupancy into a higher sea-view price and fill the wedding and events wing with premium bookings.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to SCH's research, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.75%, the 5.9% minimum wage increase to $12.85 and the 9.8% rise in food and energy input costs will affect SCH. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (5.0% to 5.75%): If SCH's $750,000 twelve-year bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage-point rise adds about $5,625 a year in interest ($750,000 × 0.75% = $5,625), lifting the fixed-cost burden above $2,490,000. Higher rates also make premium coastal breaks less tempting for cautious visitors and raise the cost of any further borrowing for the refurbishment. The direct cash impact is modest, can be capped by fixing the loan rate, and is fully computable from insert figures — unlike the other two factors, it does not erode the $83 contribution ($145 − $62) per room-night.

Minimum wage increase (5.9%, to $12.85 per hour from April 2026): Appendix 3 gives both the old and new rates, so the hourly delta is exactly $0.70 ($12.85 − $12.15 = $0.70). The exact annual cost cannot be computed from the insert, because the headcount and hours paid at the minimum wage are not stated; what can be shown is the threshold at which this factor overtakes the interest rise — it does so once SCH pays more than roughly 8,036 minimum-wage hours a year ($5,625 ÷ $0.70 ≈ 8,036), a level plainly exceeded by a seasonal 160-employee hotel across a full trading year. In Maslow's terms, financial reward helps but does not cure the 10% absenteeism driven by motivation or the 34% seasonal staff turnover, so the rise is real but manageable through engagement and productivity.

Food and energy input costs (up 9.8% year-on-year): Appendix 3 names wholesale food and energy explicitly, and SCH's $62 variable cost per room-night will include ingredients, utilities and catering. No component share is given anywhere in the insert, so the honest bound runs from $0 (if no named input applied — implausible for a full-service hotel) to a labelled upper bound of applying the whole 9.8% to the entire $62: at most about $6.08 per room-night ($62 × 9.8% = $6.08), which over the current 58,000 room-nights would cap the damage at roughly $352,640 a year (58,000 × $6.08). The true figure lies between these bounds and cannot be pinned further without inventing a share; what is certain is that every matching input rises together for every room-night sold, that SCH cannot refinance this away the way it can fix the loan rate, and that it lands precisely when the $1,200,000 refurbishment pressure is highest.

Conclusion: The 9.8% rise in food and energy input costs will have the greatest impact. Unlike the interest rise, which is exactly $5,625 a year and fixable, and unlike the wage floor, whose exposure is limited to minimum-wage hours, input inflation applies continuously to every one of the 58,000 room-nights sold and to every offer SCH makes in the domestic coastal-holiday market where consumer spending grew 4.2%. Quantifying it precisely is impossible from the insert, but even a partially exposed $62 variable cost dwarfs $5,625, and the 9.8% figure is the steepest of the two percentage rises SCH can act on for all sales volumes. SCH should respond with supplier renegotiation, waste reduction in kitchens, selective sea-view price rises (58% of researched guests accept up to $25 more) and menu engineering, while treating the minimum-wage increase — significant but smaller — as second priority and the interest-rate motion as the smallest of the three.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to SCH.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on SCH's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of SCH with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
